subtype: Approach: skill gap check against job listings [Thinking]
passage:
Monday. Ishita opened a spreadsheet and pasted in fifty job listings for the kind of role she wanted. "I keep polishing what I already know," she muttered. "Let me count what they actually ask for."
Wednesday. The tally was clear. Python, testing and databases showed up again and again, and she had those. But cloud deployment appeared in most listings, and it was not on her CV at all. "So that is why the calls go nowhere," Ishita said aloud, and highlighted the row in yellow.
Sunday. Her friend Pallavi came over with an evening course outline. They pencilled six weeks on the wall calendar, with a small project at the end that Ishita could show in interviews.

qa.q: Which skill was missing from Ishita's CV?
qa.a: Cloud deployment was missing from Ishita's CV.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when she saw the missing row highlighted in yellow?
qa.a: Ishita felt a mix of surprise and determination: she said aloud that this was why the calls went nowhere and immediately marked it.

qa.q: What could Ishita do if a course cannot fit her evenings?
qa.a: Ishita could learn the skill through a smaller weekend project, using the listings as a guide to what to cover.

qa.q: How might Pallavi see Ishita's tally?
qa.a: Pallavi may see a friend who has moved from worry to a plan, which is why bringing the course outline felt natural.

grounding: The passage shows a person reading many job listings, spotting the skill that repeats and is missing, and planning a course to close the gap.

subtype: Approach: skill gap check against job listings [Thinking]
passage:
Himani ma'am, who runs the platform team now, pulled up a chair when Ankita said the job search was going nowhere. "Twelve years ago I was laid off too, at twenty-five. For a month I applied everywhere and heard nothing. Then one weekend I stopped applying and started reading. I opened fifty listings for backend developers and made a tally on a sheet of paper.
The main language, fine, I knew it. Databases, fine. But in thirty-eight of the fifty there was one thing I had never touched: deploying to the cloud. That was my gap, staring at me.
I planned six weeks. An online course, two hours every morning, and one small project I could actually deploy and show. I felt silly starting from the basics. But in week seven I had a link to put on my CV, and the next interview asked me about exactly that."

qa.q: In how many of the fifty listings did cloud deployment appear?
How did young Himani feel starting from the basics?
qa.a: She felt silly and a bit embarrassed, but kept to the six-week plan.

qa.q: Which choice in Himani's story changed the search, and why?
qa.a: Stopping to read and tally fifty listings, because it revealed the one missing skill instead of more blind applications.

qa.q: How did the interviewer in week seven see Himani's new project?
qa.a: The interviewer found exactly the skill they were asking about, with a working link as proof.

grounding: It shows a young woman reading fifty job listings, finding cloud deployment as the repeated missing skill and planning a focused six-week course to close it.

subtype: Approach: skill gap check against job listings [Thinking]
passage:
Gurleen had three months of savings left and a one-room flat shared with two cousins, where the TV never went off. Applications weren't working. So on a Saturday, headphones on against the noise, Gurleen opened fifty listings for data engineer roles and pasted the requirements into a sheet.
Tushar, a friend from the old team, came over with samosas and helped count. "SQL, you have. Python, you have. Pipelines, you've built. But look." He pointed. "Cloud deployment. Thirty-one out of fifty. You've never done it."
Gurleen stared at the number. It was the exact thing four interviewers had asked about.
With only three months, a long certificate was out of the question. They planned six weeks instead: a free online course every morning at the library, where it was quiet, and one small project deployed by week five. Gurleen wrote the dates on the wall above the cousins' TV.

qa.q: How many of the fifty listings asked for cloud deployment?
What was Gurleen feeling while staring at the number?
qa.a: Gurleen was likely stung but also relieved to finally see the gap that four interviewers had been probing.

qa.q: Why was a six-week plan better than a long certificate?
qa.a: With only three months of savings, a short, focused course and a small project could close the gap in time to apply again.
Tushar brings an outside eye, counting the skills and pointing out the missing one, which Gurleen might have kept avoiding.

grounding: It shows someone checking fifty job listings for repeated skills, finding cloud deployment missing and planning a focused six-week course despite little money and a noisy home.
